tagline: Roof of the world in Central Asia
overview:
Tajikistan is a landlocked country in Central Asia, bordered by Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, China and Afghanistan. Mountains cover about 93 percent of it, and half the country lies more than 3,000 meters above sea level. Its area of about 143,000 km² is a little smaller than Wisconsin, but folded upward into some of the highest terrain on Earth.

About 10 million people live in Tajikistan. Tajik, a language closely related to Persian, is the state language, and Russian is widely used in government and business. Dushanbe, the capital, takes its name from the Tajik word for Monday, after the weekly market once held there.

Tajikistan is a presidential republic and one of the poorer countries in the region; many Tajiks work abroad, especially in Russia, and send money home. Aluminum, cotton and hydroelectric power from towering dams on mountain rivers are its main industries.
landAndNature: The Pamir Mountains in the east are nicknamed the Roof of the World. Ismoil Somoni Peak reaches 7,495 meters, the highest point in the former Soviet Union, and the Fedchenko Glacier is about 77 kilometers long, one of the longest outside the polar regions. The Pamir Highway climbs over passes above 4,600 meters through a cold, treeless high desert where yaks graze. Deep valleys in the west grow apricots, mulberries and cotton, and the Fann Mountains hold lakes of extraordinary blue and green. In 1911 an earthquake dammed a river and created Lake Sarez, which now holds an enormous volume of water behind a natural landslide barrier. Snow leopards, Marco Polo sheep with huge spiral horns, and ibex live in the high country.
peopleAndCulture: Tajiks are a Persian-speaking people, and their poetry, music and New Year traditions link them to Iran and Afghanistan. Navruz, the spring new year on about March 21, is the biggest festival, with families cooking sumalak, a sweet paste stirred from sprouted wheat for a whole night. Osh, or plov, rice cooked with carrots, meat and onions in a wide pot, is the dish of celebration, eaten with round flatbread that is never placed upside down out of respect. Pamiri houses have a five-pillared room and a skylight of four square frames representing earth, water, air and fire. Guests are given the best of everything. Soccer and the wrestling style gushtigiri are popular, and the national instrument, the long-necked setor, accompanies singers.
history: The Sogdians and Bactrians who lived here were traders and merchants along the Silk Road, sending goods between China and the Mediterranean. Alexander the Great's armies passed through in the 320s BC. Arab conquest brought Islam in the 700s, and the Samanid empire of the 800s and 900s, ruled from Bukhara, is celebrated by modern Tajiks as their golden age of Persian poetry and learning. Mongols, Timurids and the emirate of Bukhara followed. Russia took control in the late 1800s, and after the 1917 revolution the region became a Soviet republic in 1929, with borders drawn so that the old Persian-speaking cities of Samarkand and Bukhara ended up in Uzbekistan. Independence came in 1991, followed by a five-year civil war that killed tens of thousands before a peace deal in 1997.
funFacts: Dushanbe means Monday in Tajik, named after the Monday bazaar that once stood on the site.
The Pamir Highway is one of the highest roads in the world, crossing passes over 4,600 meters.
Lake Sarez was created by an earthquake in 1911 that dropped a mountainside across a river valley.
Tajikistan's flag flew from one of the tallest free-standing flagpoles ever built, in central Dushanbe.
The Fedchenko Glacier is so large that it holds more ice than many entire mountain ranges.
